solution.concept_anchor: GI Tag vs UNESCO ICH inscription — different protection regimes

statement_analysis.statement: A Geographical Indication (GI) Tag awarded to a tribal craft associated with a festival provides the same type of cultural protection as inscription on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage.
statement_analysis.reason: GI Tags protect the commercial and geographic identity of products (tangible outputs) under intellectual property law. UNESCO ICH inscription is a recognition and safeguarding framework for living heritage practices (intangible). These are fundamentally different protection regimes — one is IP-based product protection; the other is a cultural heritage safeguarding mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: India's ratification of the UNESCO 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of Intangible Cultural Heritage automatically confers domestic legal protection on all tribal performing arts inscribed on the Representative List.
statement_analysis.reason: Ratification of the 2003 Convention creates international obligations and recognition but does NOT automatically translate into domestic legal protection. India's domestic instruments (PESA, FRA, state laws) operate separately, and there is a documented gap between international ICH commitments and domestic implementation.

statement_analysis.statement: The Chhau dance, performed in tribal festival contexts of Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal, is classified exclusively as 'tribal' art under the UNESCO ICH framework.
statement_analysis.reason: Chhau dance has both tribal and folk dimensions — its classification blurs the tribal-folk boundary. UNESCO's 2010 inscription did not classify it exclusively as 'tribal'; it is recognised as a traditional martial dance across three states with both tribal and non-tribal practitioners.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (Statement 1 only is incorrect) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 makes the clearest false claim (conflating GI with UNESCO ICH), leading students to identify it as the only error and overlook the fabrications in Statements 2 and 3.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: GI Tags protect commercial-geographic product identity (IP law). UNESCO ICH inscription safeguards living heritage practices. These are entirely different frameworks. Statement 1 is NOT correct.

Examine Statement 2: International treaty ratification does not automatically domesticate as binding law in India — Parliament must legislate separately. The gap between UNESCO ICH commitments and PESA/FRA is documented. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Examine Statement 3: Chhau is not classified 'exclusively tribal' — it has folk dimensions and non-tribal practitioners. Statement 3 is NOT correct.
All three statements are incorrect — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the most dangerous trap: it sounds like a reasonable inference from international law. Many students believe that treaty ratification automatically creates domestic legal obligations. In India, monist-dualist doctrine means parliamentary enactment is required to domesticate international treaty obligations — ratification alone does not create enforceable domestic rights. This gap between India's 2005 ICH ratification and the domestic implementation of tribal cultural protections is precisely what the question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the intersection of international heritage law, domestic IP protection, and tribal cultural rights.
• Statement 1 — Incorrect: GI (Geographical Indication) Tags under the GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 protect the commercial-geographic identity of products — e.g., Kondapalli toys or Dhokra craft. UNESCO ICH inscription is a safeguarding framework for living intangible practices — not a product protection mechanism. These serve fundamentally different purposes.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Treaty ratification in India's legal system does not automatically confer domestic legal enforceability. The UNESCO 2003 Convention, ratified in 2005, creates international obligations but domestic laws (PESA, FRA, state art councils) must separately implement protections. The gap between India's international commitment and ground-level tribal cultural protection is well-documented.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Chhau dance (inscribed on UNESCO Representative List, 2010) is practiced across Jharkhand (Seraikella Chhau — princely court tradition), Odisha (Mayurbhanj Chhau — unmasked), and West Bengal (Purulia Chhau — with tribal roots). It blurs tribal-folk boundaries and is NOT exclusively classified as tribal.
Value Addition:
• Three styles of Chhau: Seraikella, Mayurbhanj, Purulia — only Purulia retains strongest tribal connection.
• Sangeet Natak Akademi is India's nodal body for ICH nominations to UNESCO.
• GI registration in India is administered by the Controller General of Patents, Designs & Trade Marks.

solution.concept_anchor: Seasonal sequence — Ali Aye Ligang (February) before Wangala (post-harvest)
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know Ali Aye Ligang is a spring festival (February) and Wangala is post-harvest (November) may correctly order them but invert the Mizo Pawl Kut position if they confuse it with Chapchar Kut.
elimination_logic: Ali Aye Ligang (Mising tribe, Assam): February — marks beginning of sowing season. This is the earliest in the calendar year among the three.
Chapchar Kut (Mizoram): Typically March — after jungle clearing for Jhum, before sowing. Comes after Ali Aye Ligang.
Wangala (Garos, Meghalaya): Post-harvest thanksgiving — celebrated in November after the Kharif harvest. This is the latest in the year.
Correct order: Ali Aye Ligang → Chapchar Kut → Wangala. Matches option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits confusion between Ali Aye Ligang (February) and Chapchar Kut (March) — both are spring festivals in the Northeast, separated by roughly one month. Students who know both are spring events but not their precise month may reverse them. Additionally, students may confuse Wangala's November timing with another post-harvest festival and misplace it in the sequence.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests sequential agricultural calendar awareness across three Northeast/tribal festivals.

Correct chronological order: Ali Aye Ligang → Chapchar Kut → Wangala

• Ali Aye Ligang (February): Spring festival of the Mising tribe of Assam, marking the beginning of the sowing season along the Brahmaputra. It is the earliest of the three — riverine tribe's pre-sowing celebration.
• Chapchar Kut (March): Mizoram's festival celebrated after Jhum field clearing is complete but before seeds are sown. It follows Ali Aye Ligang by approximately one month, as jungle clearing in hilly terrain takes longer.
• Wangala (October-November): Post-harvest thanksgiving of the Garo tribe, offered to Sun God Saljong. It is the most temporally distant — an autumn/winter harvest festival, not a spring event.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (b): Puts Chapchar Kut first — incorrect, it comes after Ali Aye Ligang.
• Option (c): Puts Wangala second — incorrect, it is always post-harvest (Oct-Nov).
• Option (d): Inverts all three — completely wrong.

Value Addition:
• Ali Aye Ligang: 'Ali' = seed/root, 'Aye' = fruit, 'Ligang' = sowing festival — the name itself encodes the agricultural cycle.
• Mising tribe's stilt houses (Chang Ghar) are a UNESCO-studied flood-adaptive architectural tradition.
• Wangala's '100 Drums' refers to the massed Dama drumming that accompanies the Nokma's ritual initiation.

solution.concept_anchor: Sixth Schedule ADC legislative power over social customs — festival regulation in Northeast
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) citing PESA 1996 is the strongest distractor because PESA is the most commonly studied tribal self-governance law and students may apply it without checking the geographic scope — PESA applies to Fifth Schedule areas, NOT Sixth Schedule areas like Meghalaya.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a tribal community council in Meghalaya legislating on festival practice — Meghalaya is a Sixth Schedule state with Autonomous District Councils (ADCs).

Eliminate option (a): PESA 1996 applies to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) — states like Jharkhand, Odisha, MP. Meghalaya is NOT a Fifth Schedule state; it is a Sixth Schedule state. PESA does not apply here.
Eliminate option (b): Article 29 grants individual/group cultural rights but does not vest legislative power in ADCs to make regulations.
Eliminate option (d): FRA 2006 addresses forest land rights — not legislative authority over festival regulation.

Select option (c): The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution grants Autonomous District Councils (like Khasi Hills ADC, Garo Hills ADC in Meghalaya) the power to make laws relating to social customs — which includes the governance of community festivals and cultural practices.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: PESA is the most visible tribal governance law in UPSC preparation, creating a reflexive association between 'tribal self-governance over culture' and PESA. The scope-extension trap is geographic: PESA explicitly applies only to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) Areas, which are found in states like Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana. Meghalaya is governed under the Sixth Schedule — its ADCs have direct legislative powers on social customs without needing PESA. Students who apply PESA without checking the Fifth/Sixth Schedule distinction will select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario requires identifying which constitutional provision specifically enables an Autonomous District Council in a Sixth Schedule state to legislate on tribal festival governance.

Applicable Principle: The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution (Articles 244(2) and 275) establishes Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. These councils are empowered to make laws on matters including allotment of land, management of forests, use of waterways, and — critically — social customs of the tribal communities within their jurisdiction.

• Option (a) — PESA 1996: Incorrect for Meghalaya. PESA applies only to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) — a different constitutional regime. Meghalaya operates under Sixth Schedule ADCs, not PESA.
• Option (b) — Article 29: Incorrect as the governance basis. Article 29 is a fundamental right for cultural conservation, not a legislative power-granting provision for ADCs.
• Option (c) — Sixth Schedule ADC powers: Correct. The Khasi Hills ADC, Jaintia Hills ADC, and Garo Hills ADC in Meghalaya have explicit constitutional power to make laws on social customs — including festival governance.
• Option (d) — FRA 2006: Incorrect. FRA deals with forest land rights and community forest resources, not cultural or festival regulation authority.

Value Addition:
• Sixth Schedule states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram — four Northeast states.
• Fifth Schedule covers: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, MP, AP, Telangana, Gujarat, Rajasthan, HP.
• ADCs can also establish their own courts for trying certain offences under their enacted laws — a significant autonomous judicial power.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) Nuakhai is a strong distractor because its Bhadra Shukla Panchami timing (day after Ganesh Chaturthi) creates the appearance of Hindu calendar alignment, making students think it shares the mainstream Hindu framework with option (b).
elimination_logic: Identify the shared attribute: Bastar Dussehra, Medaram Jatara, and Sarhul all have mythological or ritual foundations that are entirely INDEPENDENT of the mainstream Hindu Rama-Ravana, Durga, or agrarian-Brahminic frameworks — they are organically tribal.
Bastar Dussehra (option a): Centers on Danteshwari Mata — not the Rama-Ravana narrative. Independent tribal basis.
Mainstream Dussehra (option b): THIS is the festival centred on Lord Rama's victory over Ravana — the mainstream Hindu Ramayana narrative. It is NOT a tribal festival at all.
Medaram Jatara (option c): Centers on Sammakka-Saralamma's resistance against Kakatiya rulers — entirely tribal historical memory.

Nuakhai (option d): Although it aligns with Bhadra Panchami (near Ganesh Chaturthi), it is a first-grain offering to Samaleswari Devi — a tribal deity, representing a tribal agrarian tradition even if showing some sanskritization.
The odd one out is option (b) — mainstream Dussehra is not a tribal festival. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The question names Bastar Dussehra and mainstream Dussehra alongside genuinely tribal festivals. Students who focus on the word 'Dussehra' may conflate Bastar Dussehra with mainstream Dussehra — precisely the error the question is designed to catch. The intended trap is: students who know Bastar Dussehra is tribal may think it is the odd one out because it 'shares' a name with mainstream Dussehra. The correct identification is that mainstream Dussehra (Rama-Ravana) is the genuinely non-tribal element among tribal festivals.
solution.final_explanation:
The question asks which festival does NOT have an independent tribal mythological basis — i.e., which is NOT rooted in tribal tradition.
• Option (a) — Bastar Dussehra: Tribal. Centers on worship of Danteshwari Mata, the tribal goddess of Bastar. No Ram-Ravana narrative. 75-day duration. Gondi and Halbi communities' indigenous democratic processes (Silhadi selection) govern it.
• Option (b) — Mainstream Dussehra: This is the odd one out. It is the Hindu festival celebrating Lord Rama's victory over Ravana, rooted in the Ramayana narrative. It is not a tribal festival — it belongs to the mainstream Hindu festival calendar.
• Option (c) — Medaram Jatara: Tribal. The Koya tribe of Telangana commemorates the resistance of Sammakka and Saralamma (mother-daughter tribal heroines) against the Kakatiya dynasty. Entirely tribal historical-religious memory.
• Option (d) — Nuakhai: Tribal in origin. The first-grain ritual of western Odisha tribes (Bhuiya, Kondh, Saura) offered to Samaleswari Devi — a tribal deity showing some sanskritization but retaining tribal agricultural ceremony at its core.
Value Addition:
• Bastar Dussehra's deliberate independence from the Ramayana narrative is a point of tribal identity assertion.
• Danteshwari Mata temple at Dantewada is one of 52 Shakti Peethas — showing complex tribal-Hindu convergence.
• The Silhadi (festival officiant) selection at Bastar Dussehra is an example of indigenous participatory democratic governance.

solution.concept_anchor: Sarna religion — not all Jharkhand tribes follow it; Christian conversion among Oraon and Munda

statement_analysis.statement: The Sarna religion's festival calendar is structured around forest and agricultural cycles — beginning with Sarhul (spring new year) and moving through Karma and Sohrai — making it fundamentally different in temporal organisation from the Hindu lunar calendar.
statement_analysis.reason: Sarna's calendar is rooted in ecological and agricultural rhythms (Sal tree flowering, Bhadra month, Kharif harvest) rather than the tithi-based Hindu lunar calendar. Although some surface overlap exists (e.g., Karma on Bhadra Ekadashi), the organising principle is distinct.

statement_analysis.statement: All tribes of Jharkhand follow the Sarna religion, as it represents the pre-Christian and pre-Hindu animist tradition that has been continuously maintained without interruption across all major tribal communities of the state.
statement_analysis.reason: A significant proportion of Oraon, Munda, and Kharia tribal populations converted to Christianity through 19th and 20th century missionary activity. Not all Jharkhand tribes follow Sarna — the Christian population among these tribes is substantial, and some also follow Hinduism.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) (both correct) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is accurate and Statement 2 uses language ('pre-Christian tradition maintained without interruption') that sounds historically plausible — students who don't know the scale of Christian conversion among Jharkhand tribes may accept Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Sarna's nature-agricultural temporal organisation vs. Hindu lunar tithi-based calendar — this is a substantive and accurate structural distinction. Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that 'all tribes of Jharkhand' follow Sarna is directly contradicted by the documented Christian conversion of significant portions of Oraon and Munda populations. Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 Correct + Statement 2 Incorrect → Option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 deploys the scope-extension technique via the word 'all' — a single qualifier that converts a partially true claim into a false one. Sarna religion IS the traditional animist faith of Jharkhand tribes, and many do follow it. But the Christian mission activity in Chotanagpur (19th-20th century) converted large numbers of Oraon, Munda, and Kharia tribe members. The current religious composition of Jharkhand's tribes is mixed: Sarna followers, Christians, and some Hindus coexist. The 2011 Census data showing 50+ lakh under 'other religion' reflects only those who explicitly identified as Sarna — many tribal Christians no longer claim Sarna identity.
solution.final_explanation:
These statements test both the structural character of Sarna religion and its demographic scope among Jharkhand tribes.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Sarna organises its ritual calendar around ecological markers — the Sal tree flowering (Sarhul), the Bhadra month's agricultural midpoint (Karma), and the Kharif harvest (Sohrai). This is structurally different from the Hindu calendar's tithi-nakshatra-lunar month framework, even where calendar dates superficially overlap.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The word 'all' is the false element. Jharkhand's tribal population includes substantial Christian communities — particularly among Oraons (who were significantly converted by German and Roman Catholic missionaries from the 1840s onward) and Mundas. This is why the Sarna code demand in Census 2021 was politically significant — Sarna followers wanted differentiation from both Hindu and Christian categories.
Value Addition:
• The German Mission (Gossner Evangelical Lutheran Mission) was among the earliest to proselytise among Jharkhand tribes in the 19th century.
• Birsa Munda himself initially had contact with Christian missionaries before returning to and reforming tribal animist practice.
• The Sarna code demand: supporters argue that current Census categories force Sarna followers into 'Hindu' or 'other' — distorting population data.

statement_analysis.statement: The Andaman and Nicobar Protection of Aboriginal Tribes Regulation, 1956, legally prohibits contact with certain Andaman tribal communities, making documentation of their ritual practices impossible through official channels.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1956 Regulation (a Presidential Order under Article 371) prohibits contact with tribes like Sentinelese, Jarawa, Onge, and Shompen — officially preventing formal documentation of their ritual practices.

statement_analysis.statement: All tribal groups of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — including both Andaman and Nicobar tribes — are classified as uncontacted peoples with no historical engagement with external communities.
statement_analysis.reason: Nicobari tribes, particularly on Car Nicobar, have had historical contact with Arab traders, European missionaries, and administrators for centuries. Their Ossuary feasts and canoe rituals are documented. Conflating ALL island tribes as 'uncontacted' is factually wrong.

statement_analysis.statement: Medaram Jatara (Sammakka-Saralamma Jatara) is held biennially in February and is widely regarded as the largest tribal pilgrimage gathering in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Medaram Jatara is biennial (every two years), held in February at Medaram village, Mulugu district, Telangana, and attracts millions — making it widely described as the largest tribal religious gathering in India.

statement_analysis.statement: The historical narrative of Sammakka's resistance against Kakatiya rulers embedded in Medaram Jatara makes it a purely animist festival without any syncretic elements absorbed from Hindu tradition.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statements 2 and 4 as false may still confuse themselves about Statement 1's scope (all or some Andaman tribes) and Statement 3's 'largest' designation.

Pair 2: Nicobari tribes have documented historical contact — the 'all island tribes are uncontacted' claim is false. Incorrect.
Pair 3: Medaram Jatara biennial + February + largest tribal gathering — all elements accurate. Correct.
Pair 4: Medaram Jatara has syncretic elements (jaggery offering mirroring puja) — the 'purely animist' claim is false. Incorrect. Two pairs correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the classic conflation of all Andaman-Nicobar tribes as 'uncontacted' — when only four specific Andaman groups (Sentinelese, Jarawa, Onge, Shompen) are under contact prohibition. Nicobari tribes are contact-permitted communities with centuries of external engagement. Statement 4 exploits the narrative purity trap: students who know Medaram Jatara is a tribal resistance commemoration may assume it remains purely animist, overlooking documented syncretic elements (jaggery offerings, deity structures resembling Hindu puja).
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests precision across two distinct tribal contexts — Andaman isolation protocols and Medaram Jatara's character.

| 2 | ALL island tribes uncontacted | Incorrect |

• The Great Nicobar Island development project has raised concerns among anthropologists about Shompen welfare.

solution.concept_anchor: Miri — shaman/priest role among Adi tribe in tribal new year rituals
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 'Pahan' is a well-known tribal priest designation (from Jharkhand) that students may generalise to other tribal contexts including Arunachal Pradesh.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Deuri is a Hindu Brahmin priest category associated with Assam's mainstream Hindu temples — not the ritual specialist of the Adi tribe.
Eliminate option (b): Pahan is the tribal priest of Sarna communities (Oraon, Munda, Ho) in Jharkhand — not used by the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh.
Eliminate option (c): Garo — this is a tribe, not a priestly title. Incorrect on both counts.

Select option (d): Miri is the shaman/ritual specialist among the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, who conducts ritual proceedings including those connected to tribal new year and agricultural festivals.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap operates through well-known priestly titles from other tribal traditions. 'Pahan' (Jharkhand) is heavily studied in UPSC preparation; students may default to it when asked about any tribal priest regardless of region. 'Miri' is specific to the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh — a less-commonly tested term that requires precise knowledge of Arunachal tribal society rather than generic tribal-priest recall.
solution.final_explanation:
Tribal religious specialists play critical roles in conducting festival rituals — and their titles vary precisely by tribe and region.
• Option (a) — Deuri: Incorrect. Deuri refers to a specific caste/community of traditional priests in Assam's mainstream Hindu context — not the ritual specialist of the Adi tribe.
• Option (b) — Pahan: Incorrect. Pahan is the ritual priest of Sarna-following tribes (Oraon, Munda, Ho) of Jharkhand. Applying this title to an Arunachal tribe is a geographic-entity swap.
• Option (c) — Garo: Incorrect. Garo is a tribe of Meghalaya, not a priestly designation of any kind.
• Option (d) — Miri: Correct. The Miri is the shaman and ritual specialist among the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh. The Miri conducts ritual proceedings at agricultural festivals and new year ceremonies, embodying the indigenous knowledge system and religious authority of the community.
Value Addition:
• 'Miri' also historically referred to a sub-group of what is now called the Adi tribe — the terminology evolved post-independence.
• Adi tribe's major festival is Solung (harvest thanksgiving) — distinct from Galo's Mopin and Apatani's Dree.
• Shamans in tribal contexts bridge the living community with spirit worlds — their role in festival ritual is not merely ceremonial but cosmologically functional.

solution.concept_anchor: Instruments of Wangala — Dama, Aduri, Rangbang; Karma ecology vs gender dimension

statement_analysis.statement: The musical instruments used in the Wangala festival of the Garo tribe include the Dama (a form of drum), the Aduri (flute), and the Rangbang (gong) — together representing the core organological tradition of Garo tribal music.
statement_analysis.reason: Dama, Aduri, and Rangbang are the documented instruments of the Wangala festival — these are precisely identified in ethnomusicological accounts of Garo culture and are relevant to questions on tribal organology.

statement_analysis.statement: The Karma festival centres on the veneration of Karma tree branches brought into the village and is primarily practiced by young men who carry the branches in a procession to pray for agricultural prosperity.
statement_analysis.reason: The gender dimension is reversed — Karma festival is primarily celebrated by young women (not men) who venerate the Karma tree branches and pray for their brothers' welfare, not for agricultural prosperity.

statement_analysis.statement: The Pahan — the tribal priest of Sarna communities — occupies a role categorically different from a Brahminic priest in that the Pahan's authority derives from community selection and ecological knowledge rather than from hereditary ritual purity concepts.
statement_analysis.reason: The Pahan's authority in Sarna communities is rooted in community recognition and practical/ecological knowledge of ritual — it is fundamentally distinct from Brahminic priesthood's hereditary, purity-based authority structure.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (all three correct) is the strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are accurate and Statement 2 contains a known fact (Karma tree veneration) that makes the whole statement appear correct to students who don't notice the gender reversal.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Dama, Aduri, Rangbang as Wangala instruments — correctly stated, ethnomusicologically documented. Correct.
Statement 2: 'Young men... agricultural prosperity' — both elements are wrong. Karma is primarily by young women for brothers' welfare. Incorrect.
Statement 3: Pahan's authority from community selection and ecological knowledge vs. Brahminic hereditary purity — accurately captures the distinction. Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 embeds two errors while retaining the accurate core (Karma tree veneration). First, the gender is reversed — the festival is women-centered, not men-centered. Second, the purpose is misdescribed — it is for brothers' welfare, not agricultural prosperity. A student who knows Karma involves tree veneration but hasn't studied the gender and purpose dimensions will accept Statement 2 as partially correct and select option (d) or (b), depending on their confidence in Statement 3.
solution.final_explanation:
Three important tribal cultural details are tested here across tribal music, ritual gender roles, and priestly authority.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Wangala's three signature instruments — Dama (large barrel drum), Aduri (bamboo flute), and Rangbang (gong) — constitute the core of Garo tribal music during the festival. The '100 Drums' designation comes from the massed Dama drumming at the Nokma's ritual initiation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Two errors. (i) Karma festival is primarily observed by young women — not men. Women venerate the Karma tree branches installed in the village. (ii) The purpose is for brothers' well-being and long life — not agricultural prosperity. Agricultural themes are secondary.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Pahan (Sarna community priest) derives authority from community consensus and practical ritual knowledge, including knowledge of the sacred grove (Sarna), appropriate timing of ceremonies, and interpretation of signs. This contrasts sharply with Brahminic priests whose authority is hereditary and based on ritual purity (varna-based).
Value Addition:
• Rangbang (gong) in Wangala is distinct from Chinese or Southeast Asian gongs — it is locally forged and has specific ritual uses.
• Karma tree (Nauclea parvifolia or Haldina cordifolia) is a real species — its ritual significance reflects animist ecology.
• The Pahan-Brahmin distinction is relevant to debates about indigenous religious autonomy under Article 25 (freedom of religion).

solution.concept_anchor: Fifth Schedule vs Sixth Schedule — different legal frameworks for tribal cultural protection
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is the strong distractor because both A and R are correct, and students may assume PESA's application to Fifth Schedule naturally explains the different governance regimes, not realising this is the precise causal claim being evaluated.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes — Fifth Schedule tribes (mainland) and Sixth Schedule tribes (Northeast) operate under different legal frameworks. Fifth Schedule tribes are governed through Governors' powers and PESA/Gram Sabhas; Sixth Schedule tribes through Autonomous District Councils with direct legislative powers.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? Yes — PESA 1996 applies specifically to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas) — it does NOT apply to Sixth Schedule states like Meghalaya, Assam, Tripura, and Mizoram, which have their own ADC framework.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? Yes — the existence of PESA as a Fifth-Schedule-specific law is precisely the mechanism that creates the different framework for festival governance. Fifth Schedule tribes have Gram Sabha powers under PESA; Sixth Schedule tribes have ADC legislative powers. R explains A.

Both A and R are correct, and R explains A → correct option is (a). Wait — re-reading: R states PESA does NOT extend to Sixth Schedule areas. This is the reason for the different frameworks. Does R explain A? Yes — the non-extension of PESA to Sixth Schedule (and the existence of ADC powers instead) is exactly what creates the 'different legal frameworks' described in A. Correct option is (a).
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests the constitutional architecture of tribal cultural protection across the two major Schedule frameworks.

Assertion (A) analysis: Correct. Fifth Schedule (mainland tribal areas: Jharkhand, Odisha, MP, Chhattisgarh, AP, Telangana, Gujarat, Rajasthan, HP) and Sixth Schedule (Northeast: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) represent two distinct constitutional frameworks for tribal governance. In Fifth Schedule areas, the Governor has special powers; Gram Sabhas are empowered through PESA. In Sixth Schedule areas, Autonomous District Councils have direct legislative authority.

Reason (R) analysis: Correct. PESA 1996 was enacted specifically to extend Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) Areas — it explicitly does not apply to the Northeast states governed under the Sixth Schedule. This is not a gap in PESA — it is by design, as Sixth Schedule ADCs already had constitutional legislative powers.

Causal relationship: R does explain A. The reason Fifth and Sixth Schedule tribes operate under different governance frameworks for festival and cultural management is precisely because PESA is a Fifth-Schedule-specific legislation, and Sixth Schedule states have their own ADC framework under Articles 244(2) and 275. The two frameworks are constitutionally parallel, not hierarchical.

Value Addition:
• The Bodoland Territorial Council (Assam) is a Sixth Schedule body with significant cultural governance powers.
• Governors of Fifth Schedule states have special tribal advisory councils (Tribes Advisory Councils) to advise on tribal welfare.
• Art. 338A establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes — distinct from NCM, as earlier discussed.

statement_analysis.statement: Bara Deo is the supreme deity in Gondi cosmology, while Persa Pen is the village deity worshipped in the Madai festival — these are two distinct entities within the Gondi religious pantheon.
statement_analysis.reason: Gondi cosmology does distinguish between Bara Deo (the supreme/sky deity, also called Bada Dev) and Persa Pen (the village guardian deity taken in procession during Madai). These are distinct deities with different ritual roles.

statement_analysis.statement: Bastar Dussehra's governing structure includes the Silhadi — a ritual officiant chosen through indigenous democratic processes by the tribal communities — making it distinct from mainstream Dussehra events managed by government bodies.
statement_analysis.reason: The Silhadi (also rendered as 'Silhadi pujari') is indeed selected through community processes — a form of tribal participatory governance embedded in the festival's ceremonial structure.

statement_analysis.statement: The Bison Horn Maria are a sub-group of the Gond community named after the buffalo (bison) which is their primary sacrificial animal during festivals, and they are found predominantly in the Abujhmar hills of Chhattisgarh.
statement_analysis.reason: Two errors: (i) The name refers to the bison-horn headdress worn in ritual dances — not the buffalo as a sacrificial animal; (ii) The Bison Horn Maria are found in Bijapur and Dantewada districts of Bastar, NOT in the Abujhmar hills — the Abujhmar hills are the domain of the Hill Maria sub-group.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) (1, 2 and 3) is the strong distractor, but actually 1 and 2 are correct here. Let me reconsider — the question asks which are correct. Statements 1 and 2 are correct, Statement 3 is incorrect. The answer should be option (a) 1 and 2 only.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Bara Deo (supreme) vs Persa Pen (village deity, Madai) — distinct deities correctly differentiated in Gondi cosmology. Correct.
Statement 2: Silhadi selection through community processes at Bastar Dussehra — documented feature of the festival's indigenous governance. Correct.

Statement 3: Two errors — (i) the name 'Bison Horn Maria' refers to the bison-horn headdress used in dances, not a sacrificial animal; (ii) Bison Horn Maria are in Bijapur-Dantewada (south Bastar), NOT Abujhmar hills (where Hill Maria live). Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the entity-swap between Bison Horn Maria (Bijapur-Dantewada, south Bastar) and Hill Maria (Abujhmar hills, Narayanpur). Both are Gond sub-groups; both are in Chhattisgarh. The geographic assignment is swapped. Additionally, the 'sacrificial animal' explanation for the name is a plausible-fabrication — the name actually derives from the bison-horn headdress used in ritual dances (a tangible material culture item), not from any sacrificial practice.
solution.final_explanation:
This question demands sub-group-level precision within the Gond community and accurate details about Bastar's festival governance.
• Statement 1 — Correct: In Gondi cosmology, Bara Deo (Bada Dev) is the supreme sky deity — akin to the highest cosmological principle. Persa Pen is the village guardian deity who is taken in procession between villages during the Madai — a mobile deity distinct from the supreme deity.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Bastar Dussehra's Silhadi is a ritual officiant position filled through community selection — an example of tribal participatory governance embedded in festival structure. This distinguishes it from state-managed or temple-trust-managed festivals.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Two factual errors. First, the Bison Horn Maria are named after the bison-horn headdress worn by dancers in ritual performances — not after any sacrificial practice involving buffalo/bison. Second, they inhabit Bijapur and Dantewada districts (south Bastar) — NOT the Abujhmar hills. The Abujhmar hills are the relatively isolated habitat of the Hill Maria sub-group.
Value Addition:
• Abujhmar hills (Narayanpur district) are one of India's least-administered areas — Hill Maria live there with limited government contact.
• Bison Horn Maria's ritual dances with horn headdresses are among the most visually distinct tribal performance traditions in India.
• Gond sub-groups: Bison Horn Maria (Bijapur-Dantewada), Hill Maria (Abujhmar), Muria (Kondagaon-Bastar), Dorla (Sukma), Halba (broader Bastar).

elimination_logic: Item A (Po:Rong): Traditional rice beer of the Mising tribe of Assam — central to Ali Aye Ligang festival. Match with 3.
Item B (Yaping Hurlo): Apatani women's traditional nose plug — discontinued cultural body modification from Arunachal Pradesh. Match with 4.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap operates between Mising (Assam) and Garo (Meghalaya) material culture items. Po:Rong (Mising rice beer) and Dama drum (Garo) are both Northeast tribal items — students may conflate them, especially because both tribes have Brahmaputra basin connections. solution.final_explanation:
This question tests knowledge of tribal material culture items and their precise community associations.

Correct Matches:
• A (Po:Rong) — 3 (Mising tribe, Assam, Ali Aye Ligang): Po:Rong is the traditional rice beer of the Mising tribe, prepared and consumed during Ali Aye Ligang. It is a central element of their festive material culture.
• B (Yaping Hurlo) — 4 (Apatani women, Arunachal Pradesh, discontinued): Yaping Hurlo is the traditional nose plug worn by Apatani women as a cultural body modification practice. Now discontinued, it was historically used as a tribal identity marker.
• C (Dama) — 1 (Garo tribe, Meghalaya, Wangala '100 Drums'): Dama is the large barrel drum of the Garo tribe. The Wangala festival's popular name — '100 Drums Festival' — derives from the massed Dama drumming at the Nokma's ritual initiation.
• D (Ponung) — 2 (Adi tribe, Arunachal Pradesh, agricultural festivals): Ponung is a ritual group dance performed by Adi women during festivals including Solung. It is often confused with Mopin (Galo) — a frequent UPSC trap.

Trap: Po:Rong (Mising, Assam) vs Dama (Garo, Meghalaya) is the geographic-swap — both Northeast, different states and tribes.

Value Addition:
• Mising stilt houses (Chang Ghar) and Po:Rong together represent the ecological and material culture of a riverine tribe.
• Apatani women's tattoos (facial tattoos + Yaping Hurlo) were reportedly adopted to make women less attractive to raiding tribes — an anthropological theory now contested.
• The Adi tribe's Solung (harvest) festival is distinct from Mopin (Galo) — both Arunachal but different communities.
